It is recited as "uhiya" (أحي). Its origin is "wuhiya" (وحي); one says "awha ilayhi" and "wahha ilayhi," and the waw is changed into a hamza, as one says "a'idu," "a'zinu," and "wa-idha al-rusulu uqqitat" (﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾). This is from the unrestricted substitution (al-qalb al-mutlaq), which is permissible in every dammed waw. Al-Mazini also allowed it in the kasra-marked waw, as in "ishah" and "isadah" and "i'a akhihi." Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "wahya" in its original form.

"Annahu istama'a" (أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ) with a fatha, because it is the agent of "awha" (the verb is "awha"). "Inna sami'na" (إِنَّا سَمِعْنا) with a kasra, because it is an inceptive clause (mubtada') narrated after a verb of saying. Then the remaining instances are assimilated to these two: whatever is part of the revelation takes a fatha, and whatever is the speech of the jinn takes a kasra.

All of them are from the speech of the jinn except the two last ones, "wa-anna al-masajida" and "wa-annahu lamma qama." Whoever reads all of them with a fatha takes them as a conjunction on the place (mahall) of the prepositional phrase in "amanna bihi," as if it were said: "We believed in him and we believed that He, exalted is the majesty of our Lord, and that he, our foolish one, used to say..." and likewise the rest.

﴿A group of the jinn﴾: a company of them, numbering between three and ten. It is said they were of the Shayatin, who are the most numerous of the jinn and the general soldiers of Iblis.

﴿So they said, "We have heard"﴾: that is, they said to their people when they returned to them, like His saying: ﴿And when it was decreed, they turned to their people as warners. They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses..."﴾ [46:29–30]. ﴿A wonderful Qur'an﴾: wondrous, unique, distinct from all other books in the beauty of its composition and the soundness of its meanings, in which the proofs of its inimitability (i'jaz) are established. "'Ajab" is a verbal noun placed in the position of the adjective "'ajib" (wondrous), and it carries hyperbole: it is that which has gone beyond the limits of its kind and its like.

﴿It guides to the right course﴾: it calls to what is correct. It is said: it calls to monotheism (tawhid) and faith. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an. Since believing in it is believing in Allah, in His oneness, and in disassociation from polytheism, they said: ﴿And we will never associate anyone with our Lord﴾: that is, we will never return to what we were upon of associating others with Him in obedience to Satan.

It is permissible that the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because His saying "our Lord" explains it. "Jadd Rabbina" (جَدُّ رَبِّنا) means His greatness, from your saying: "jadda fulan fi 'aini" (so-and-so became great in my eye), i.e., he grew great. In the hadith of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "When one of us recited al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, he became great among us" (جدّ فينا). And it is narrated "fi a'yunina" [[I have not seen it from 'Umar; rather it is from Anas, as has passed in al-Baqarah.]]. Or it means His kingdom and authority. Or His wealth, a metaphor from "jadd," which is fortune and prosperity, because kings and the wealthy are those who are fortunate. The meaning: He is described as exalted above having a consort or a son, because of His greatness; or because of His authority and dominion; or because of His richness. His saying ﴿He has taken neither a consort nor a son﴾ is an explanation of that.

It is also read "jaddan Rabbina" (جدًّا ربنا) as a specifying accusative (tamyiz). And "jaddu Rabbina" with a kasra (بالكسر) means: the truth of His lordship and the rightness of His divinity, free from taking a consort or a son. That is because when they heard the Qur'an and were guided to monotheism and faith, they became alert to the error in what the disbelieving jinn had believed about God, namely likening Him to His creation and taking a consort and a son, so they magnified Him and declared Him free of it.

﴿Their foolish one﴾: Iblis, may Allah curse him, or another of the rebellious jinn. ﴿Shatat﴾ means exceeding the limit in wrongdoing and other things. From it comes "ashatta fi al-sawm," when one goes far in the price. That is: he says a statement which in itself is shatat (excessive), because of how far he exceeded in it, which is attributing a consort and a son to Allah. We had thought that no one among humans or jinn would lie against Allah or fabricate about Him what is not true, so we believed them in what they attributed to Him of that, until the Qur'an made clear to us their lying and fabrication.

﴿A lie﴾: a false statement, i.e., something falsely said. Or it is in the accusative of the verbal noun, since lying is a kind of speech. Whoever reads "an lan tuqawwil" (أن لن تقوّل) places "kadhiban" in the position of "taqawwul" (fabrication) and does not make it an adjective, because fabrication can only be a lie.

*Traces back to a lineage among his people, not lowly."*

*Our paternal cousins to be noble of beds."*

Or it is an expression by the name of the place for what is in it, namely the wives, as a *majaz mursal*. The nobility of women is blameworthy, because it is an allusion to immorality, just as their stinginess is used to refer to their chastity. So we are not equal in the mothers.

It is said: *lamasahu*, *iltamasahu* and *talammasahu*, like *talabahu*, *atlabahu* and *tatallabahu*. Similar to these is *al-jass* (feeling out, searching). *"I fear a little man or a riding camel going out at dawn,*
*And the wolf I fear, and a barking dog."*

That is: and I fear the wolf, and a barking dog conjoined to it. Or it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: and I fear a barking dog. The clause is conjoined to the clause "I fear a little man." The mention of the dog as *'awiyan* (barking) serves as a warning, lest it be suspected that he is lying in his claim.

Because *al-rajul* and *al-rakb* are singular nouns with the meaning of the plurals *al-rijal* and *al-rikab*. *Al-rasad* is like *al-hars*: a collective noun for *al-rasid* (watcher), in the sense of: "the ones possessing a flaming meteor, watching for stoning," namely the angels who stone them with shooting stars and prevent them from listening. *"...and a stomach hungry (ma'an jiaan)..."*

Its meaning: he finds a meteor watching over him and for his sake.

*"The wild ass, its trail covered with dust, and its foal*
*Races behind them, darting like a shooting star.*

*Above them rose a long, extended cloud of dust,*
*As if its mist were dust raised by roosters that love it,*
*Or a dark cloud, or the tanabaa'* (?)... "

*"So they raced a slow course like it,*
*Far off is their course and the colt's course."*

These lines are by Bishr ibn Abi Khazim. *Al-'ir* means the male donkey. *Yurhiquha* means he burdens her, that is, the she-ass. *Al-jubar* (with an unpointed letter, and it is said with its vowel pronounced otherwise) means the trace of anything; with a pointed letter it means soft ground. It is also narrated as *al-ghubar* (dust). *Al-inqidad* means speed. *Al-sabt* means the extended dust. *Al-dabab* means dew covering the ground in the early mornings. *Al-sad* is the cock that scratches the earth and raises its dust; it is also applied to a measure of copper or of a cooking vessel, and to a disease of the head treated by cauterization with fire. It is said also that it means the flag, and this is the meaning given here. *Al-dawajir* are the sudden ones, from *dajara* when one becomes lively with joy; or the darkened ones. *Al-layl al-dujur* and *al-dayjur* mean the dark night. *Tandub* is the name of a tree whose smoke is white, and it is the name of a village near Makkah. *Al-shaw'* means the running course; it is said *shaʼa* like *sahā*, when one outstrips another. *Al-tawlab* is the colt when a year has passed over it.

He says: the wild donkey burdens its she-ass with following its trail while running, and its foal hastens behind her, as the speed of a shooting star. A long extended dust rose above them, as if the misty part of it were dust raised by roosters, which love it; and as if it rose from a dark tanabaa' tree, or a darkness, because it veils the light even though it is white; so *dawajir* is a predicate after a predicate.

It is also permissible that this is with the conjunction omitted. Al-Sirafi, Ibn 'Asfur (Ibn Asfur) and Ibn Malik permitted this, while Ibn Jinni and al-Suhayli prohibited it, and they explained what seems to imply it as a *badal al-idrab* (a substitution of correction). This is also permissible here: he compared the rush to three things, then he said: "they raced a long course like it," and affirming distance for the like is a kinaya for affirming it for the course. It is possible that the pronoun in *mithlihi* refers to the foal, so it is in the accusative. Then he said: "after the distance between their course and his course, as if he lagged behind." It is possible that the meaning is: after each of the two courses, and it was long.

*"It dived like a glittering star, followed by*
*A dust cloud that rises, which you take to be a tent-rope."*

This is by Aws ibn Hajar, describing a horse with intense speed and swiftness. *Ka-l-durri* (like a glittering star) is in reference to its pearl-like qualities, or it is derived from *al-dar'* (repelling), because it repels darkness. *Yatba'uhu* means the horse; *naq'* means dust that spreads. You suppose it to be a *tunub* (with two vowels), which is the rope of the tent, just as its ray follows the glittering star extended at its fall. So he likened the dust to the tent-rope explicitly, and to the star's ray implicitly.

*"The wild ass returns to us, away from its mate,*
*Or the wild bull, like a glittering star followed by blood."*

This is by Awf ibn al-Kharra', describing a horse with intense speed in hunting, and that a wild ass is turned back by it, in a state where... that is, the donkey is away from its mate, that is, near it; or it turns it back from behind it, that is, from its vicinity. It is also permissible that the meaning is: the donkey is without its mate, that is, alone, with no companion to bring it confusion. Or the wild bull returns to us, in a state where it, the bull, is like a glittering star. Or the horse is like a glittering star, that is, like a star named after the pearl for the purity and brightness of its essence. Or it is from *al-darah* (repelling), that is, repelling, because it repels darkness, in a state where the star, as it falls from the sky, is followed by a red line of its light resembling blood. So "blood" is an explicit metaphor.

However, the devils used to eavesdrop at certain times. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, the stoning increased and grew into a clear increase, so that both humans and jinn became aware of it, and eavesdropping was entirely prevented.

From Ma'mar: I said to al-Zuhri: "Were stars thrown in the pre-Islamic period?" He said: "Yes." I said: "What do you make of His saying ﴿And we used to sit there in ambush﴾?" He said: "It became severe and its matter was intensified when the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent."

Al-Zuhri narrated from Ali ibn al-Husayn, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting with a group of the Ansar, a star was thrown and it lit up. He said: 'What did you used to say about the like of this in the pre-Islamic period?' They said: 'We used to say: a great one dies, or a great one is born.'"

[Muslim narrated it from the narration of al-Awza'i from al-Zuhri from Ali ibn al-Husayn from Ibn Abbas: "Men of the Ansar informed me," and he said: "While they were sitting," and mentioned it at length. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the narration of Ma'mar from al-Zuhri from Ali ibn al-Husayn from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While..." and mentioned it, but he did not say "informed me" (men of the Ansar).]

In His saying ﴿ملئت﴾ (they were filled) there is evidence that the occurrence is the filling and abundance. Likewise His saying ﴿nakud minha maqa'ida﴾ (we used to sit in them in places): that is, we used to find some of the seats empty of the guards and the meteors, but now all the seats have been filled. This mentions what impelled them to travel throughout the lands until they came upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and listened to his recitation.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 72, verse 11:

﴿Among us are the righteous﴾: among us are the pious and the God-fearing. ﴿And among us are those who are otherwise than that﴾: among us are a people who are otherwise than that. So the qualified noun is omitted (ḥadhf al-mawṣūf, ellipsis of the noun being described), as in His saying ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾. They are the ones who are moderate in righteousness, not perfect in it.

Or they meant the wicked: ﴿we were divided into various ways﴾ is an explanation of the division mentioned. That is: we were people of differing, separated paths. Or: in the variety of our conditions we were like the different paths. Or: we were on different paths, as in his saying:

*As the fox hurries along the road* [[The explanation of this line was given earlier in part two, page 92; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

Or our paths were ﴿various ways﴾, with the omission of the genitive construct (muḍāf) which is "the paths," and the pronoun in the place of the construct's annexed noun taking its position. The word *qidda* derives from *qadda*, as *qiṭʿa* (piece) derives from *qiṭaʿ* (pieces). The paths were described as *qidad* (divided, separated) because it indicates the meaning of being cut off and scattered.

In the earth and as fugitives are two circumstantial phrases (ḥālān). The meaning: we will not frustrate Him while we are in the earth, wherever we are in it, nor will we frustrate Him by fleeing from it to the heavens. It has also been said: we will not frustrate Him in the earth if He intends a matter concerning us, and we will not frustrate Him by flight if He seeks us. Here ẓann (supposition) carries the sense of yaqīn (certainty). This describes the states of the jinn, and the conditions and beliefs they hold:

Among them are the righteous, the wicked, and those in between; and they believe that Allah, mighty and majestic, is the All-Mighty, the Overpowering, from whose pursuit nothing escapes and from whom no refuge can save.

لَمَّا سَمِعْنَا الْهُدَى ﴿When we heard the guidance﴾, meaning their hearing of the Qur'an and their belief in it. ﴿فَلَا يَخَافُ﴾ ﴿so he does not fear﴾, meaning: he does not fear. That is, he is not afraid. Because the sentence is structured as a subject (mubtada', the topic) and a predicate (khabar, the comment), the fa' (the particle "fa") was introduced. Without that, it would have been said: "lā yakhaf" (he does not fear, jussive). If you ask: what is the benefit of putting the verb in the indicative (raf') and positing a subject before it so that it becomes its predicate, and of making the fa' obligatory, when all of that could be dispensed with by saying "lā yakhaf"? I answer: the benefit is that when it is expressed this way, it is as if it were said: "So he does not fear." This indicates the certainty that the believer is saved without doubt, and that this is specific to him and not to anyone else.

al-A'mash recited ﴿فَلَا يَخَفْ﴾ (fa-lā yakhaf) in the jussive as a prohibition (nahy). ﴿بَخْسًا وَلَا رَهَقًا﴾ ﴿any loss or any burden﴾, meaning: a recompense of loss or burden, because he has not deprived anyone of a right, nor has he burdened anyone with injustice [[His saying "nor has he burdened anyone with injustice": in al-Sihah, "rahiqahu" (with kasra) "yarhaquhu rahaqan" means "ghashiyahu," that is, he overtook him or covered him.]]. So he does not fear the recompense for either of them. In this there is an indication that it is the right of one who believes in God to avoid wrongdoing. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 72, verse 16–17:

﴿And that, if they had remained upright on the path﴾: "Anna" is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of "anna" (the heavy form, an-nathqilah), and this clause is part of what was revealed. The meaning: "It was revealed to me that the matter and the report are that, if the jinn had remained upright upon the most excellent way"; that is, if their father, the jinn (al-Jann), had persisted in what he was upon of worshipping God and obedience, and had not been arrogant toward prostrating to Adam, nor disbelieved, and his offspring had followed him in Islam, then We would have bestowed favour upon them and widened their provision. He mentioned "abundant water" (al-ma' al-ghadaq), meaning much, read with a fatha and with a kasra on the dal.

It is also read with both (vowels), because it is the foundation of livelihood and the abundance of provision. ﴿That We might test them therein﴾: that We might try them therein, to see how they would give thanks for what they were granted from it. It is permissible that its meaning be: "And that, if the jinn who listened had remained upon their way which they were upon before hearing [the Qur'an] and had not turned away from it to Islam, We would have widened provision for them, leading them on gradually (mustadrijin lahum), so that We might test them therein": that the blessing would be a cause for their following their desires, falling into trial, and increasing in sin; or that We would punish them for their ingratitude for the blessing.

﴿Whoever turns away from the remembrance of his Lord﴾: from His worship, or from His admonition, or from His revelation, ﴿He will make him enter (yaslukhu) a severe punishment﴾. It is read with a nun, damma and fatha; that is, "We shall cause him to enter a punishment." The original is "naslukuhu fi 'adhab," as in His saying, ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾, so it takes two objects: either by omitting the preposition and making the verb reach it directly, as in His saying, ﴿and Musa chose his people﴾; or by its being made to carry the meaning of "to cause to enter," as one says "salakahu" and "aslakahu." A poet said:

*Until, when they caused them to enter Qutā'idah*
*[Qutā'idah: in al-Sihah, the name of a pass. Abd Manaf ibn Rab' said:*
*"Until, when they caused them to enter Qutā'idah, they drove them off as a herd of camels drives off the scattered ones."*
*Al-shall means driving away; al-shurud is the plural of shārid, as khadam is the plural of khādim. (Ibn Manzur?)]*

The *sa'ad* is the verbal noun of *ṣa'ida* (to ascend); one says *ṣa'ida ṣa'adan wa ṣu'udan*, and so it is used as a description of punishment, because the punished one is overcome by it: it rises over him, overpowers him, and he cannot bear it. From this is the saying of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "Nothing has been as burdensome to me (ma tasa'adanī shay'un) as the marriage proposal sermon (khutbat al-nikah)." [Abu 'Ubaydah related it in al-Gharib from the narration of Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father from 'Umar with this wording, and it is disconnected (munqati').] He means: it was not difficult for me nor did it overcome me.

It was also said: it is the plural of masjid, which means the act of prostration (sujud).

**"The servant of God" (ʿabd Allāh) is the Prophet (ﷺ).** If you ask: why was it not said "the Messenger of God" or "the Prophet"? I answer:

Because its underlying sense is: "And it was revealed to me that when the servant of God stood..." Since it occurs within the speech of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about himself, it is expressed in the way that humility and self-abasement require.

Or because the meaning is that the worship of the servant of God toward God is not something far-fetched to the intellect or objectionable, such that they should "almost be piled upon him in a mass" (libadan).

The meaning of ﴿قَامَ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ يَدْعُوهُ﴾ ("the servant of God stood calling upon Him") is: he stood worshipping Him. He means his standing for the dawn prayer at Nakhla, when the jinn came to him and listened to his recitation (ﷺ).

﴿كَادُوا يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِ لِبَدًا﴾ ("they almost became a mass upon him"): that is, they crowded upon him, piled up in amazement at what they saw of his worship and the imitation of his companions of him, standing, bowing and prostrating, and in admiration of what he recited of the Qur'an, because they saw what they had never seen the like of, and heard what they had never heard the like of.

It has also been said that its meaning is: when he stood as a messenger worshipping God alone, differing from the polytheists in their worship of gods other than Him, the polytheists almost crowded upon him, piling up in a mass, because of their collusion against him and their cooperation in enmity toward him. *Libadan* is the plural of *libda*, which is what has matted together, one part upon another, and from it comes "the mane of the lion" (*libdat al-asad*). It is also read *lubdan*, and *al-libda* carries the same meaning as *al-libda*. *Libadan* is a plural of *labid*, like *sajid* and *sujud*. *Lubudan* (with two damma-vowels) is the plural of *labud*, like *saboor* and *sabr*.

From Qatada: "The humans and the jinn clustered together against this matter to extinguish it. But God refused except to support it and make it prevail over whoever opposed it."

As for the one who reads *wa-innahu* with a kasra (i.e., *wa-innahu* as the beginning of a separate clause), he makes it part of the speech of the jinn: they said it to their people when they returned to them, recounting what they had seen of his prayer and of his companions crowding upon him in following him in prayer.

Say, "I only call upon my Lord, and I associate no one with Him." (Qur'an 72:20)

This is what the commentator means: "I have not brought you anything reprehensible. I only worship my Lord alone and I do not associate anyone with Him, and that is not something that should make you unite against my hatred and enmity." Or he said to the jinn when they crowded around him in amazement: "What you see of my worship of God and my rejection of association with Him is not a matter to be amazed at; rather, one should be amazed at the one who calls upon other than God and makes partners for Him." Or the jinn said this to their people, relating the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿Nor can I bring you harm or benefit (rashadan)﴾ (Qur'an 72:21). Or he meant by "harm" misguidance (al-ghayy), and this is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "neither misguidance (ghayyan) nor guidance (rashadan)." The meaning is: I am not able to harm you or to benefit you; rather, the one who harms and benefits is God. ["He, may God be exalted, said: 'The meaning is: I am not able to benefit you or harm you; rather, the one who benefits and harms is God, mighty and majestic...' (Mahmud) I say: In the verse there is clear evidence that God, exalted is He, is the one who owns for His servants guidance and misguidance, that is, He creates them, and no other. For the Prophet (ﷺ) only negated that from himself so that its attribution would be purely to the power of God alone. Zamakhshari perceived this and began to manipulate the matter: sometimes he takes "guidance" to mean general benefit, and so attributes that to God, exalted is He; and sometimes he evades it, because in it is the annulment of the specific sense of guidance mentioned explicitly in the verse, so there arise in him from his imitation of a corrupt opinion upheavals that divert him from the truth and from the belief that God, exalted is He, is the one who creates guidance for His servants concurrently with their choice, so he introduces the notion of compulsion (qasr), because the meaning of what is reported about attributing guidance to the power of God, according to them, is that He creates for the one over whom that power has subjugated necks, so the servant creates for himself guidance when it appears, and it is attributed to the power of God, because He created the cause, which in reality is created by the power of the servant. This is the principle and creed of the Qadariyya; and the jinn, after this, were only more perceptive than them and more sound in reasoning, for they said: 'And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance,' attributing guidance itself to the will and power of God, mighty and majestic.]"

Or: I am not able to compel you to misguidance or guidance; rather, the one capable of that is God, mighty and majestic.

﴿Except a message from God⦆ (Qur'an 72:23). This is an exception from what precedes: I possess nothing except a message from God.

["He (Mahmud) said: 'It is an interjection. And His saying "except a message" is an exception from His saying "I do not possess", meaning: I do not possess for you except a message. It was also said: "a message" is a substitute for "refuge"...' I say: The sense of the statement would then be: a message from God, derived from His saying: 'Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a distant term.']

And "Say: Indeed, no one will protect me from Him" is a parenthetical clause, interposed to emphasize the negation of his capability and to declare his helplessness, meaning: if God intends for him some harm, such as illness, death, or other, no one can grant him protection from it, nor find besides Him any refuge to which he may flee.

Al-multahad means the place of refuge; its root meaning is "the entrance," from al-lahd (the niche of a grave). It was said: an escape or a way out. It was also said: "I do not possess" is read "qala" (he said), meaning that the servant of God said to the polytheists or to the jinn. It is permissible that it is from the jinn's report to their people. It was also said that "a message" is a substitute for "refuge": that is, I will not find besides Him any deliverance except that I convey from Him what He sent me with. It was also said: "illa" here is "in la" (if not), and its meaning is: that I do not convey a message, as in your saying: "if not standing, then sitting." "And His messages" is conjoined to "a message", as if it were said: I do not possess for you except conveying and messages; the meaning being: except that I convey from God, saying: "God said such-and-such," attributing it to Him, and that I convey His messages which He sent me with, without addition or subtraction.

If you say: Could one not say "balagh 'anhu" (convey from him)? And from it is his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "Convey from me, convey from me." ["Reported by al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As with the wording: 'Convey from me even a single verse...' (the hadith)."]

I say: "min" here is not a complement of conveying; rather, it is in the sense of His saying: "A disavowal from God" (bara'atun min Allah), meaning: a message issuing from God.

It is read: "fa-inna lahu nara jahannam" (so indeed for him is the fire of Hell), on the basis of: "fa-jaza'uhu anna lahu nara jahannam" (so his recompense is that for him is the fire of Hell), like His saying: "fa-anna lillahi khumusahu" (so that for God is one-fifth of it), meaning: so its ruling is that one-fifth belongs to God.

He said "khalidina" (abiding), taking it in light of the plural sense of "man." If you say: With what is "hatta" (until) connected, and what follows it made its goal? I say: With His saying "yakununa 'alayhi libadan" (they would almost crowd upon him), meaning that they would collectively oppose him with enmity, belittle his helpers, and consider their numbers insignificant, "until, when they see what they are promised" from the Day of Badr and God's manifestation of victory over them, or from the Day of Resurrection. "Then they will know at that time that they are weaker in helpers and fewer in number."

It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element indicated by the situation: the disbelievers' belittling of him and their regarding his numbers as insignificant, as if it said: they will continue in their condition "until, when they see what they are promised." The polytheists would say: "When will this promised thing be?" as a denial of it. So it is said: "Say: It is certainly coming, there is no doubt about it, so do not deny it, for God has promised that, and He does not break His promise. As for its time, I do not know when it will be, for God has not specified it, since He saw in concealing its time a benefit."

If you say: What is the meaning of His saying "or will my Lord set for it a distant term" when a term may be near or far? Do you not see His saying: "She wishes that between her and it were a great distance"? I say: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to regard the appointed time as near, so it is as if he said: I do not know whether it is a condition expected at every moment, or a deferred matter for which a limit has been set, that is: He is the Knower of the Unseen, so He does not reveal it, does not let anyone know of it.

"Of a messenger" (min rasulin) is a specification of "those He approves," meaning: no one knows the Unseen except the one approved, who is chosen for prophethood specifically, not every approved person. In this there is a refutation of miracles (karamat) ["His saying 'and in this there is a refutation of miracles': refuting them is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, while affirming them is the doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunna, and they are not restricted to reports of the Unseen. (A'.)"], because those who are attributed to them, even if they are approved friends, are not messengers. ["Mahmud said: 'a refutation of miracles, because He restricted that to the approved of the messengers, while the friend, even if among the approved...' I say: He claimed a general matter and proved it with a specific one, for his claim is the refutation of miracles in all their kinds, while what the verse indicates is only the refutation of a friend's knowledge of the Unseen; and no miracle or departure from custom is other than knowledge of the Unseen alone. The Qadariyya have a doubt in refuting them, namely that God, mighty and majestic, never takes them as friends, and they never reported this from their followers, so they will persist in denial and do not know that the condition of a miracle is friendship with God, which is denied them by consensus. As for denying faith, that is a matter of disagreement; so I do not expect one whose faith is a matter of dispute to desire miracles, since he was not granted them. And God is the Granter of success.]"

God has specified the messengers from among the approved with knowledge of the Unseen and the refutation of soothsaying and astrology, because their practitioners are the furthest thing from approval and the most deserving of wrath.

﴿For He sends before him and behind him guards﴾ (Qur'an 72:27). "Before him" means before the one approved for the message, and "behind him guards": guardians from the angels who protect him from the devils, drive them away from him, and safeguard him from their whisperings and confusions until he conveys what was revealed to him. It is reported from al-Dahhak: No prophet was sent except that angels were with him to guard him from the devils, lest they take the form of an angel.

﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾ (Qur'an 72:28), meaning the prophets. He first used the singular in the words "before him and behind him," then the plural in the sense, as in His saying: "Indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein," and the meaning is: that they may convey the messages of their Lord as they are, guarded from addition and subtraction. The mention of knowing is like its mention in His saying: "until We know the strivers." It is also read "liya'lama" (that He may know) in the passive voice.

﴿And He encompasses what is with them﴾, meaning what the messengers have of wisdom and laws; nothing of it escapes Him, and He forgets not a single letter of it; He is the Guardian over it, the Protector of it. ﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾ (Qur'an 72:28), of rain drops, sand, leaves of trees, and foam of seas. How then would He not encompass what the messengers have of His revelation and speech?

"Adadan" is a circumstantial accusative, meaning: and the regulation of everything counted and enumerated; or it is a verbal noun in the sense of counting.
